The thing about that is, how do you pronounce jpeg? I've never heard it pronounced j-feg, always j-peg, despite photo being pronounced as if it started with an f.

That said, I still pronounce gif with a hard g.

P never sounds like F unless it's PH, and there's no H in JPEG.

You'll notice the G in JPEG is hard, too.

I think what's really going on here is what we intuitively consider 'normal' vs 'exceptional': We see P and we think the sound in the word pop, or prove, or play. Only when we see the H do we think it's the F sound. For those who see G, some think of hard G as the default and some thing of soft G as the default, and are only willing to override when prompted externally.

Even if we made up a nonsense word from scratch, we'd look for cues in it that remind us of other words.

In fact I think this is the biggest reason why the majority ended up supporting the hard-g pronunciation. GIFT. it's one letter away from GIF. Are there any other words close to GIF?

Meanwhile, we look at JPEG. Can't pronounce the J, so we just say it out loud. But Peg is a word! We know the word peg, we say it all the time, so naturally it just slides right in.

I realize that p only sounds like f with a ph, but the argument was that gif should have a hard g because graphics has a hard g, and if you're using that argument then jpeg should still be pronounced jpheg, because photo is pronounced as if it were with an f.

The point, though, is that it is not just that one factor. There are multiple factors contributing to the pronunciation of file types as either acronyms or initialisms.

[✔] supports current pronunciation, [✘] opposes current pronunciation.

GIF:
[✔] More closely resembles existing word, "Gift," which has a hard G.
[✘] Originator says it's a soft G
[✔] Majority of people default to hard G when they see the letter G and there is insufficient information to cause them to override this.
(Furthermore, there is another dedicated letter that represents the soft-G sound {J} and they explicitly decided not to use it here.)
[✔] Base word for acronym itself uses a hard G.

JPEG:
[✔] Contains an entire word with a known pronunciation.
[✔] Originator claims hard-p pronunciation is correct.
[✔] Default pronunciation of P as hard variant is almost entirely universal in English.
[✘] Word base for acronym uses soft P sound.
(but that word base requires the usage of a second letter to modify the sound {H} which is not even present in the acronym.)

EXE:
[✔] There are no words that particularly resemble this arrangement to give us a clue as to a word-like pronunciation, and as such all attempts are left sounding really awkward.
[✘] To the best of my knowledge, the person who came up with it never expressed an opinion on the pronunciation as the enumeration of its letters.
[✔] We're used to initialisms in our culture like FBI, SOS, NHL, for things that also don't give us a clue as to words they might resemble. Fuh-Bee? Soas? N'Hull?
[✘] The E sound in Executable is a shorter e than the sound we make when referring to the letter itself.
(Despite the fact that we know the word Executable, saying "Ekseh" without the rest of the context fails to ring memory associations, and could more easily be confused with other things with the same vowel layout. Like "Eggs" in a funny accent.)

And if we cancel out word bases AND originator claims on all of these, we STILL get overwhelming momentum for their present most-used colloquialisms. it's not about what's "right" anymore, it's just about what is. Our entire argument is kind of moot, but I still enjoyed discussing it with you.

There's a long history of not pronouncing abbreviations using the phonetics of the root words. There's also a long history of not pronouncing things the way they "should" be based solely on spelling. Incidentally, soft or hard Gs are usually determined by the following vowel: a soft i or e is usually preceded by a soft G. Note all the "usually"s: there are a bunch of exceptions to that, too.

The person who invented the word, and the people in that environment, used one pronunciation. Once it got out of that closed environment, other people who had only read it but never heard it before had to decide how to pronounce it. Some of them went with the hard G, some with the soft.

Consult a quality dictionary and you will find many many words with multiple pronunciations. You will find many words where the pronunciation differs from origin words. You will find many words that begin with or include both hard and soft G sounds. You will find both pronunciations of GIF listed.

With so many counter-examples, the only possible way to determine a "correct" pronunciation is the only thing without a contradicting example: the creator (and namer) of the format did not explicitly state that both a hard G and a soft G are correct, only a soft G. However, both hard and soft G sounds have become acceptable through widespread use, so it's kind of an asinine argument to be having at all.
